6960:
Christian movements have commissioned women preachers at various times: Quakers (Margaret Fell's Women's Speaking Justified, 1666), early Methodists, the Salvation Army (Catherine Booth), nineteenth-century holiness movements and early Pentecostalism. Mainline denominations began ordaining women in the twentieth century (e.g. American Methodists and Presbyterians granted full clergy rights in 1956; the Church of England ordained women priests in 1994 and bishops from 2014-15).

Evangelical egalitarianism as a named movement arose in the 1970s and 80s. Christians for Biblical Equality (CBE) was organized in 1987, led by Catherine Clark Kroeger and others, and in 1989 published 'Men, Women and Biblical Equality'. Unlike secular feminism, CBE affirms biblical inerrancy and argues from Scripture. Its scholars have produced detailed work on kephalē, authentein, text criticism of 1 Cor 14 and the history of Junia. Egalitarians differ among themselves on method, from those who read the restrictive texts as purely local, to 'redemptive-movement' readings (William Webb) that trace a trajectory beyond the letter of the text.
6961: Women and men equally bear God's image and received the creation mandate together.
6962: Hierarchy between the sexes is a result of the fall, described in Gen 3:16, not part of God's creational design.
6963: In Christ and through the Spirit, ministry is distributed by gifting, not sex.
6964: Scripture records women exercising authority over men as prophets, judges, apostles, deacons and teachers with divine approval.
6965: The restrictive texts address specific local problems and should be read in light of Paul's wider practice.
6966: Marriage is a partnership of mutual submission and shared authority.
6967: Restricting women's ministry hinders the church's mission and contradicts its baptismal theology.
6968: Male and female together bear God's image and together receive dominion; no hierarchy is mentioned.
6969: 'He shall rule over you' describes a tragic consequence of sin, not a divine command or a pre-fall ideal.
6970: Deborah judges all Israel and commissions Barak, a woman with God-given authority over men.
6971: The Spirit falls on sons and daughters, male and female servants, who all prophesy.
6972: Unity in Christ removes sex as a criterion for standing and service in the church.
6973: Phoebe the deacon and patron, Prisca the co-worker named before her husband, and Junia 'outstanding among the apostles'.
6974: Paul gives husband and wife symmetrical authority over each other's bodies, a radical mutuality.
6975: Whatever priority Paul notes, 'in the Lord' man and woman are mutually dependent and both come from God.
6976: Submitting to one another frames the household code, which then subverts Roman patriarchy.
6977: Women should learn; the prohibition targets women domineering or teaching error in Ephesus, not all women for all time.
6978: God himself appointed women over men (Deborah, Huldah), and Paul names women as co-workers, a deacon and an apostle; a universal ban on women's authority cannot be reconciled with these approved examples.
6979: 1 Cor 11:5 assumes women pray and prophesy publicly, so 14:34-35 cannot be an absolute rule; text-critical evidence of displacement suggests it may not be original at all.
6980: 1 Timothy addresses a church where false teachers targeted women (5:13-15; 2 Tim 3:6-7) and forbade marriage (4:3), which explains the odd reference to childbearing in 2:15.
6981: If women are permanently barred from authority because Eve was deceived, it implies women are more deceivable by nature, which complementarians themselves deny; the argument is therefore illustrative, not ontological.
6982: The church moved beyond the household codes' acceptance of slavery by following the gospel's trajectory; the same logic applies to women, as nineteenth-century abolitionist-feminists argued.
6983: Women preached and led in the early Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal revivals with evident fruit, and the Greek Fathers recognized Junia as an apostle.
6984: 'Equal in worth but permanently subordinate in role by birth' is hard to distinguish from inequality when the role is assigned solely by an unchangeable trait.
6985: Egalitarian readings rely on speculative reconstructions of Ephesian or Corinthian backgrounds, while Paul explicitly grounds his instruction in Genesis, not local conditions.
6986: The interpolation theory for 1 Cor 14:34-35 has no manuscript that omits the verses; displacement is not omission.
6987: The slavery analogy fails: Scripture never grounds slavery in creation, but it does ground male headship in creation (Gen 2) and in Christ's relation to the church (Eph 5).
6988: Egalitarianism treats ministry as a function assigned by gifting and so misses that ordination configures the priest to Christ the Bridegroom; the question is not competence or rights but sacramental sign.
6989: Evangelical egalitarianism lacks a principle of tradition: a near-unanimous practice of East and West for two millennia is set aside on the strength of recent lexical and background studies.
6990: Paul's own letters supply the background: 1 Timothy repeatedly mentions women swayed by false teaching. Reading Genesis as a local analogy (Eve deceived, like these women) is as textual as reading it as a universal rule, and fits Paul's illustrative use of Eve elsewhere (2 Cor 11:3).
6991: Many egalitarians (e.g. Keener) accept the verses as authentic and read them as addressing disruptive questions. The interpolation argument is supplementary: no manuscript omits them, but scribal sigla and the Western displacement are genuine data that Fee and Payne have documented.
6992: Pro-slavery theologians did argue from creation and the curse (Gen 9:25) and from apostolic household codes. Gen 2 says nothing about authority; hierarchy appears first in Gen 3:16 as a result of sin.
6993: Protestants read the New Testament as presenting ministers as servants of word and sacrament, not sacrificing priests; the only priests named are Christ (Hebrews) and all believers (1 Pet 2:9; Rev 1:6). If priestly representation is real, Christ's humanity, not maleness, is what it signifies.
6994: Egalitarians respect tradition but note that it also contains women deacons, abbesses, prophetesses and Greek patristic praise of Junia; and that past restrictions often rested on claims about women's weaker reason that no tradition now affirms.
6995: Egalitarians deny any difference between men and women.
6996: The subtitle of the movement's flagship volume, Discovering Biblical Equality (2004), is 'Complementarity Without Hierarchy': egalitarians affirm sexual difference but deny that it determines authority or office.
6997: Egalitarianism is secular feminism imported into the church.
6998: Evangelical egalitarians argue from Scripture, often affirm inerrancy, and trace their roots to revival movements centuries before modern feminism.
7000: Egalitarian scholars have written some of the most detailed studies of 1 Tim 2 (Payne, Kroeger, Westfall, Belleville); they disagree on interpretation, not on its authority.
7001: Released many women into preaching, pastoral and missionary leadership, especially in Pentecostal and holiness movements.
7002: Prompted rigorous research on Junia, Phoebe and women in early Christianity.
7003: Promoted mutual submission in marriage, which advocates link to healthier dynamics and lower tolerance of abuse.
7004: Helped churches reflect on cultural assumptions read into Scripture.
7005: Critics argue its hermeneutic can be extended to justify other revisions of biblical ethics.
7006: Has contributed to denominational splits and tensions in ecumenical relations with Catholic and Orthodox churches.
7007: Some argue it underplays the theological meaning of sexual difference.
7008: Background-heavy arguments can leave ordinary readers dependent on specialist reconstructions.
7010: Assemblies of God (ordains women) and many Pentecostal churches
7011: Church of the Nazarene, Wesleyan Church, Free Methodist Church, Salvation Army
7013: Most mainline Protestant churches (United Methodist, ELCA, PC(USA), Church of England)
7014: Many evangelical scholars and seminaries (e.g. Fuller, Asbury)
7015: Sacramental view (Catholic and Orthodox male priesthood)
7016:
The Catholic and Orthodox churches ordain only men as priests and bishops, but their primary reason is sacramental rather than a general hierarchy of men over women. In the Eucharist the priest acts in persona Christi, in the person of Christ the head and Bridegroom of the Church. Because sacraments work through natural signs (bread, wine, water, oil), the bodily sign of the minister matters: a male priest represents Christ the Bridegroom offering himself for his Bride, the Church. Christ freely chose twelve men as apostles, and the Church holds that it has no authority to alter what he instituted.

The view denies that this exclusion implies any lack of dignity, holiness or ability in women. The greatest of creatures in Catholic and Orthodox devotion is a woman, Mary the Theotokos, who was not an apostle or priest. Women serve as abbesses, theologians, Doctors of the Church, missionaries and, historically in the East, ordained deaconesses. In marriage, recent Catholic teaching (John Paul II's Mulieris Dignitatem, 1988) reads Eph 5 as mutual subjection out of reverence for Christ, so this view can be called complementarian without a domestic chain of command. Catholic teaching treats the reservation of priesthood to men as definitively held; Orthodox churches hold the same practice but with less formal definition and some open discussion.
7018: The Supplement to his Summa Theologiae (compiled after his death from his commentary on the Sentences) argues that a sacrament is a sign and must signify what it confers, and holds that the female sex cannot receive holy orders. Modern magisterial teaching relies less on his arguments about women's 'state of subjection' and more on sacramental sign.
7021: Developed a 'theology of the body' and a positive account of the 'feminine genius'. In Mulieris Dignitatem he read Eph 5 as mutual subjection; in Ordinatio Sacerdotalis he declared that the Church has no authority to confer priestly ordination on women and that this judgment is to be definitively held.
7024: Dean of St Vladimir's Orthodox Theological Seminary. He edited a widely read volume of Orthodox reflection on women and the priesthood, arguing from the Bridegroom symbolism of Christ and the distinct vocations of men and women in the Church's life.
7027: Metropolitan of Diokleia and Oxford lecturer. His essay on man, woman and the priesthood of Christ defended Orthodox practice, but his later revisions and his dialogue with Elisabeth Behr-Sigel acknowledged that the theological reasons are not settled and that the question deserves open study.
7029: Catholic theologian (Missionary Servant of the Most Blessed Trinity)
7030: American theologian who once supported women's ordination and later became a leading expositor of the magisterial position, explaining Inter Insigniores and Ordinatio Sacerdotalis for general readers and answering common objections.
7031:
For most of history the male priesthood was simply practised, not defended at length, and older arguments often included claims about women's subjection or weakness that the churches no longer use. The modern sacramental argument took shape in response to Protestant and Anglican ordination of women. In 1976 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith issued Inter Insigniores, approved by Paul VI, giving three main reasons: Christ's free choice of men, the constant tradition of the Church, and the 'natural resemblance' between Christ and the priest who acts in his person. In 1994 John Paul II's Ordinatio Sacerdotalis declared the matter definitively settled for Catholics, and in 1995 the CDF stated that this teaching belongs to the deposit of faith.

In Orthodoxy, an inter-Orthodox consultation at Rhodes (1988) reaffirmed the male priesthood while recommending revival of the female diaconate. Orthodox theologians differ on the reasons, and figures such as Elisabeth Behr-Sigel argued the question is open. The Catholic Church has twice (2016, 2020) set up commissions to study women deacons. Anglo-Catholics, and some Lutherans, hold related sacramental views; C. S. Lewis's essay 'Priestesses in the Church?' (1948) is a well-known Anglican statement.
7032: Men and women possess equal dignity and are equally called to holiness; baptism confers a common priesthood on all the faithful.
7033: The ministerial priesthood is a sacramental sign, not a right or a reward for ability.
7034: The priest acts in the person of Christ, head and Bridegroom of the Church, and the minister's maleness belongs to that sign.
7035: Christ freely chose only men as the Twelve, though he broke social conventions regarding women in other ways.
7036: The constant tradition of East and West is a binding witness the Church cannot set aside.
7037: Marriage is a communion of mutual self-giving rather than a hierarchy of command.
7038: Women's vocations, including consecrated life, teaching, and in many places the diaconate, are integral to the Church.
7039: Jesus calls 'those whom he desired' and appoints the Twelve; a free choice that the Church takes as normative for the apostolic ministry.
7040: 'Do this in remembrance of me' is addressed to the Twelve at the Last Supper and understood as the institution of the priesthood.
7041: Christ is Bridegroom and the Church is Bride; the priest stands sacramentally for the Bridegroom offering himself.
7042: The marriage of the Lamb shows that the nuptial symbolism of salvation is eschatological, not merely cultural.
7043: Priesthood is received by divine call, not taken by right; 'no one takes this honour for himself'.
7044: All the baptized share a royal priesthood, distinct in kind from the ministerial priesthood.
7045: Mary's free consent makes her the model disciple and Mother of the Church, a dignity higher than priesthood though she was not ordained.
7046: Phoebe the diakonos is cited in support of the historic female diaconate, a distinct ministry from priesthood.
7047: Mary Magdalene is sent to announce the resurrection to the apostles, honoured in tradition as 'apostle to the apostles'.
7048: Jesus acted freely toward women (speaking with the Samaritan woman, accepting women disciples, entrusting the resurrection announcement to women), so his choice of only men for the Twelve was not cultural compulsion.
7049: Sacraments signify by natural resemblance; just as bread and wine cannot be replaced by other foods, the minister who represents Christ the Bridegroom must be male for the sign to be what Christ instituted.
7050: Despite women's prominence in the early church (deaconesses, martyrs, patrons), no orthodox church ordained women priests; groups that did, such as some Montanists or Collyridians, were treated as deviant by Epiphanius and others.
7051: Even the Mother of God, the most honoured of creatures, was not made an apostle or priest, showing that exclusion from orders is not a judgment on worth.
7052: The nuptial pattern of salvation (Hos 2; Eph 5; Rev 19) gives sexual difference theological meaning that the liturgy enacts.
7053: The Church is the steward, not the owner, of the sacraments; it cannot change the matter or minister of a sacrament any more than it can change the words of institution.
7054: The New Testament never calls Christian ministers priests (hiereis) offering sacrifice; Christ's once-for-all sacrifice ended sacrificial priesthood, so 'in persona Christi' lacks biblical grounding.
7055: Resting the matter on tradition and church authority rather than on Paul's explicit creation-order texts makes the conclusion depend on a doctrine of the Church that Protestants reject.
7056: If the minister must resemble Christ's maleness, women seem less able to image Christ, which threatens the patristic principle that 'what is not assumed is not healed': Christ assumed human nature common to both sexes.
7057: Christ also chose only Jewish, free men; selecting maleness alone as normative is arbitrary. And historic arguments for exclusion relied on claims of women's inferiority that the churches now reject.
7058: Evidence of ordained deaconesses, and of Junia among the apostles, shows the tradition was less uniform than claimed.
7059: Catholics and Orthodox read Christ's one sacrifice as made present, not repeated, in the Eucharist (Mal 1:11 as patristically read; 1 Cor 10:16-21). The Fathers from the early second century (e.g. Ignatius, the Didache) speak of the Eucharist as a sacrifice and of ordered ministers.
7060: Scripture is read within the Church that produced and canonized it; reliance on tradition is not a substitute for Scripture but a way of reading Christ's own institution of the Twelve.
7061: Christ's humanity saves all; the question is not salvation but sacramental sign. Women image Christ in holiness and image the Church as Bride, the role every Christian, male or female, shares in relation to Christ.
7062: Jewishness belonged to the old covenant's preparatory stage, deliberately opened to Gentiles in Acts; slavery is a social status, not created nature. Sexual difference belongs to creation (Gen 1:27) and to the nuptial covenant. The magisterium has dropped arguments from inferiority and relies on sign and institution.
7063: Deaconesses were a distinct order with specific tasks (assisting at women's baptisms, catechesis), and their existence is fully compatible with the reservation of priesthood; their possible revival is an open question precisely because diaconate and priesthood differ.
7064: Catholics and Orthodox exclude women from priesthood because they think women are inferior or unclean.
7065: Official teaching grounds the practice in sacramental sign and Christ's institution and explicitly affirms women's equal dignity; inferiority arguments of earlier writers are not part of current teaching.
7066: The sacramental view is the same as evangelical complementarianism.
7067: It does not rest on a general principle of male authority; it concerns the sacramental priesthood, and its account of marriage stresses mutual self-gift. Many lay roles of teaching and governance are open to women.
7068: Women have no leadership in these churches.
7069: Women lead religious orders, universities, hospitals and dioceses' offices; four women are Doctors of the Church (Teresa of Ávila, Catherine of Siena, Thérèse of Lisieux, Hildegard of Bingen); the Orthodox calendar names women 'equal to the apostles'.
7070: Gives theological meaning to embodiment and sexual difference rather than treating the body as irrelevant.
7071: Separates the question of ordination from claims about competence or worth.
7072: Sustained vast networks of women's religious orders in education, healthcare and mission.
7073: Provides continuity with the practice of the ancient church across East and West.
7074: Many Catholic and Orthodox women report experiencing the exclusion as a judgment on them, whatever the official rationale.
7075: Has been a major obstacle in ecumenical relations with Anglicans and Protestants who ordain women.
7076: Declaring the matter definitively settled limits open theological discussion within Catholicism.
7077: Critics argue the 'natural resemblance' argument gives sacramental weight to maleness in a way that is hard to square with a common human nature.
7080: Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian)
7082: Many Anglo-Catholics and the Polish National Catholic Church
7083: Some confessional Lutherans who hold a strong view of the pastoral office
7085: The man is formed first and given the command before the woman exists; the woman is made as a 'helper fit for him' and named by him. These details, which Paul himself cites (1 Tim 2:13; 1 Cor 11:8-9), establish a pre-fall pattern of male responsibility that sin distorts but does not create.
7087: 'Helper' ('ezer) is used most often of God helping Israel (Exod 18:4; Ps 121:1-2) and implies no subordination; kenegdo means 'corresponding to' or 'facing' him. The point of the story is the man's incompleteness without a partner of his own kind. Order of creation proves nothing, since animals were made before Adam.
7089: Read with the Fathers and with John Paul II's theology of the body, the passage reveals a communion of persons: two distinct, complementary ways of being human who find themselves in mutual self-gift. Sexual difference is meaningful and iconic, preparing for the nuptial mystery of Christ and the Church, but it is not primarily a ranking.
7090: Paul forbids women to teach doctrine authoritatively or to exercise authority (authentein) over men in the gathered church. Authentein, a rare word, most naturally means 'exercise authority' in a neutral sense; syntax with oude pairs it with the positive activity of teaching. The grounds in 2:13-14 are creational, not cultural, so the rule is permanent.
7091: Authentein is a hapax with a range including 'domineer' or 'assume authority one does not have' (the KJV's 'usurp authority'). Paul writes to Ephesus where false teachers were exploiting women (1 Tim 5:13-15; 2 Tim 3:6-7); the present-tense 'I am not permitting' addresses that crisis. Women must first learn (2:11), which was itself radical, and then may teach as Priscilla did.
7092: The verse belongs to apostolic order for the liturgical assembly and has historically been read as excluding women from the presiding and preaching office tied to the priesthood. But the Catholic magisterium does not rest the male priesthood mainly on this verse; Inter Insigniores treats Paul's disciplinary rules as partly culturally conditioned while the sacramental reservation is not.
7093: Kephalē ('head') here carries the sense of authority, as Grudem's survey of Greek usage argued. The triad (Christ head of man, man head of woman, God head of Christ) shows that headship and equality coexist, since Christ is equal to the Father yet submits. Women may pray and prophesy (11:5) but should signal the man's headship.
7094: Kephalē can mean 'source' or 'origin' (as of a river), which fits Paul's argument from origin in 11:8-12 ('woman came from man... man comes through woman'). Others read 'prominent one'. Paul's real concern is shameful dress in worship, and he explicitly balances any priority with mutual dependence 'in the Lord' (11:11-12).
7095: Head imagery is ordered to the Christ-Church mystery. The Fathers read 11:3 within Trinitarian and nuptial theology; the verse supports a symbolic, iconic order in worship rather than a general rule that every man governs every woman.
7096: This cannot be absolute silence, since 11:5 assumes women prophesy. The most likely sense (Carson, Grudem) is that women should not take part in the authoritative weighing of prophecies (14:29), which would place them in a judging role over male prophets. 'As the Law says' points back to the creation order. Every known manuscript contains the verses.
7097: Fee argued the verses are an early marginal gloss: in a group of Western witnesses (Codex Claromontanus, Augiensis, Boernerianus, some Old Latin, Ambrosiaster) they stand after 14:40, and a floating text often indicates an insertion. Payne adds manuscript sigla in Vaticanus and Victor of Capua's correction in Codex Fuldensis. Even if authentic, the verses address disruptive questioning, not women's ministry.
7098: The Church has read these verses as a discipline about liturgical order; the tradition never took them as forbidding women to speak at all (women sang, prophesied, and later preached in some settings). They are not the foundation of the male priesthood, which rests on Christ's choice and sacramental representation.
7099: In context (3:23-29) Paul speaks of equal standing as heirs in Christ through faith. Equal access to justification does not erase every distinction: Paul elsewhere still gives distinct instructions to husbands and wives. 'No male and female' echoes Gen 1:27 but addresses salvation status, not church office.
